text:
A: Hiya! Agnieszka, Wolverhampton.
B: Alright? Gareth, Taunton. Nice to meet you.
A: You too. Can I ask, that machine behind you, is dialysis, yeah? I saw in the photo.
B: Yeah, home haemodialysis. Five sessions a week, about four hours each. The spare room's basically a little clinic now. Kidneys gave up about three and a half years ago.
A: Four hours, five times. That's like a part-time job.
B: [laughs] That's what I tell people. Pays worse, mind. I was a civil engineer before, flood defence mostly, but I had to stop.
A: And you do it yourself, the needles and everything?
B: Yeah. You get trained up at the unit for a few months, then they let you loose. Hannah, my partner, she helps set up on bad days. She's a SENCo at a primary school, so she's well used to looking after people.
A: Oh, primary! I work in primary school office, in Tettenhall. Front desk, attendance, dinner money. So I know the SENCo, always running, always with papers.
B: That's her. Her marking and paperwork lives on our kitchen table. I have to eat round it.
A: [laughs] Our SENCo is same. Is the busiest person in the school, I think. So what do you eat? Is a special diet, no?
B: Very. Low potassium, low phosphate, and I can only drink about a litre a day. I weigh everything and log it on an app. Bit obsessive, but it works.
A: Potassium, so no tomatoes? Oh no. I grow tomatoes, this year so many, I was going to say I send you some.
B: [laughs] I'm allowed a few. A slice or two, carefully. Bananas are the real enemy. And I miss proper cheddar. And crisps. And a cold pint. Being thirsty all day is the worst bit, honestly.
A: That's hard. My husband, he can't go two hours without tea.
B: It does sort of focus the mind. I'm on the transplant list, two years now, so that's the hope.
A: Family can't give, like a brother or something?
B: My brother got tested. Wasn't a match. So, erm, it's the list.
A: Okay. I hope it comes soon. I mean it.
B: Cheers. Appreciate that. What about you, you've been here a while? I'm guessing Poland?
A: Yeah, Łódź. Since 2006. First two years I was cleaning offices, then college, bookkeeping, then the school. Now is eighteen years, my kids grew up here. My son is at uni in Leeds, my daughter doing A-levels.
B: That's a proper journey. Do you get back much?
A: Once, twice a year, my mum is there. I drive sometimes, sometimes fly from Birmingham. I don't mind long drives.
B: Lucky. Travel's a whole spreadsheet for me now. I have to book dialysis at a unit wherever we go, so it's Cornwall, the Lakes. If it's not near a unit, we don't go.
A: But you still go. That's the important thing.
B: Yeah, that's how Hannah puts it. And we take the dog. Biscuit, old Border terrier. Refuses to walk if it's raining, so not much use in the Lakes.
A: [laughs] Clever dog. He knows.
B: He does. Sits down on the canal path and just looks at me.
